newsitem.title: GERMANY: GERMAN EMU READINESS FACES FRESH QUESTION.
newsitem.headline: GERMAN EMU READINESS FACES FRESH QUESTION.

text.p: Germany's ability to qualify for monetary union was called into fresh question at the weekend amid reports of a possible jump in the budget deficit and public resentment of the single currency project.
The respected Der Spiegel weekly magazine said the government itself saw a risk of the country's 1997 budget deficit posting a surprising climb beyond levels allowed for joining EMU.

Internal calculations at the Chancellor's office show the budget deficit climbing as high as 4.15 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, Der Spiegel said in a release ahead of publication on Monday.

A German government spokesman denied the report, saying the Chancellor's office had not made such calculations, but the article could still unnerve financial markets when trade opens on Monday morning.
The figure is well beyond the three percent level mandated by the Maastricht Treaty for joining monetary union and is also above the government's official target of 2.9 percent.
The German deficit stood at 3.8 percent last year.
Such a high deficit would mean that even under a liberal interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty, Germany would not make the first wave of currency union planned for 1999.
EMU is scheduled to start on January 1, 1999, but the decision as to who can join will be made in the first part of 1998 on the basis of 1997 figures.
A survey published on Saturday, meanwhile, showed that a majority of Germans are against EMU.
The Infratest Burke financial research institute said only 37 percent of Germans accepted the planned currency union, while 57 percent were against it, the Welt am Sonntag newspaper reported.

Of those against EMU, most were worried that the planned currency, the euro, would be weaker or less stable than the deutschemark, while others feared that Germany would end up carrying the financial burden of EMU.
An adviser to former economics minister Karl Schiller, Wilhelm Hankel, added his voice to the euro-doubters chorus.
In a newspaper interview Hankel said Germany would fail to meet Maastricht Treaty deficit targets and that Europe could do without adopting a single currency.
"One cannot pull the euro-train into the station if the roadbed is not stable," Hankel said.
Despite obstacles in getting ready for monetary union, Spiegel said, finance minister Theo Waigel would use the German budget to help Germany will qualify.

The magazine said Waigel expects to be able to cut the apparent size of the budget deficit by calculating in a 10 billion surplus in pension contributions, eight billion marks from nursing care insurance and 1.75 billion marks in Bundesbank profits.
Government building projects, meanwhile, could be financed privately, allowing the government to delay actual spending beyond this year.

Several members of the Bundesbank council have spoken out against using "accounting tricks" to qualify for monetary union, saying they would threaten confidence in the future European currency, the euro.
